cultivar: Blend of Wuyi cultivars (typically Shui Xian and Rou Gui plus others), or pure Qi Dan / Bei Dou
processing: Medium oxidation (roughly 30–50%) built up by repeated shaking through the night, then fixed, rolled into twisted strips and charcoal roasted in one to three passes over the summer. Most commercial lots are blends (pinpei) tuned to a house roast.
harvest_season: One spring picking, usually late April to mid-May, taken as mature shoots with three or four open leaves (kai mian); there is no autumn harvest of any importance.
appearance_dry: Long, tightly twisted dark strips, matte brown-black with the odd reddish edge and a toasty, sweet smell.
appearance_liquor: Deep orange to amber, bright and clear, darker with heavier roasts.
appearance_wet: Thick, leathery olive-brown leaves with reddened rims (the classic green leaf with a red border), slow to unfurl fully.
taste_profile: Roast and warm caramel first, then baked stone fruit and dried plum, finishing on a flinty, cooling mineral note that sits in the throat; good lots stay smooth with no charcoal bitterness.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, a porcelain gaiwan or a zisha pot kept for roasted oolong. Fill the gaiwan about two thirds with dry leaf, pour fast and decant completely; a quick rinse is optional. If it tastes burnt, the tea is too fresh from the roaster rather than badly brewed: let it rest a few months.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year: picked once in spring, roasted over the summer and released once the fire has settled, so the new tea reaches shops from roughly September onward. Lightly roasted lots are best within a year; medium and heavy roasts improve after six months of rest and hold for two to five years sealed and dry. Older lots are sold as aged yancha with the year stated, and anything called mother-tree Da Hong Pao is a story, since those trees have not been picked since 2006.
description:
Da Hong Pao is the headline name of Wuyi rock tea (yancha), grown on the cliffs and in the gorges of the Wuyi Mountains in northern Fujian. What makes it distinct is less one bush than a whole style: a mature-leaf oolong, charcoal roasted, with the mineral, throat-cooling quality drinkers call yan yun (rock rhyme) that comes from thin soils over weathered volcanic rock and plots shaded by cliff walls.

Almost none of the Da Hong Pao on the market comes from the six famous mother trees on the Jiulongke cliff, which stopped being harvested in 2006. What you buy is either a pure-bred Da Hong Pao, usually the Qi Dan or Bei Dou cultivars propagated from those trees, or, far more often, a blend that a tea maker assembles from Shui Xian, Rou Gui and other Wuyi cultivars to hit a house profile. A good blend is a craft product, not a cheat; a lazy one is a way to use up leftovers.

The leaves are picked mature, withered in the sun, shaken repeatedly to bruise the edges and oxidise them partway, then fixed, rolled into strips and roasted over charcoal, sometimes three times across the summer. Roasting is what turns bruised green leaf into something dark, warm and layered, and it is also where the tea's age clock starts: a fresh roast is sharp and smoky, a rested one is round.

In the cup expect roast first (toasted grain, caramel), then fruit (dried plum, baked peach) and a long mineral aftertaste. Lighter roasts show more florals and fruit; heavier roasts are smoother and more cocoa-like but need months of rest. Brew with boiling water, plenty of leaf and short steeps; the leaves hold eight or more infusions and the later ones are where the sweetness lives.

When buying, ask about roast level, harvest year, whether it is a blend or a single cultivar, and where it grew: zhengyan tea from the core scenic area costs several times more than banyan or outer-mountain tea, and the word Da Hong Pao alone tells you nothing about that. To understand what the blend is built from, drink a Rou Gui and a Shui Xian side by side first.
sources_note: Oxidation percentages are rough trade figures. The 2006 end of picking from the Jiulongke mother trees is widely reported; blend composition varies by maker.
